lessons.title: Reading Furniture Blueprints and Technical Drawings
lessons.body: A furniture blueprint is a map for building. In Africa, many workshops rely on hand-drawn sketches, but learning to read standard technical drawings opens doors to bigger contracts and accurate work. Start by identifying the three main views: front, top, and side. Each view shows the same piece from a different angle. Lines matter: thick solid lines are visible edges, dashed lines are hidden edges (like a shelf inside a cabinet), and thin chain lines are centerlines for drilling. Dimensions are usually in millimeters. For example, a chair seat might be 450mm wide, 400mm deep, and 450mm high. Always check the scaleâ1:10 means every 10mm on paper equals 100mm in real life. A title block in the corner tells you the project name, scale, and date. Learn to read a cutting list: it lists each part, its dimensions, and quantity. For a simple stool, you might have four legs (40x40x450mm), one seat (400x400x20mm), and four stretchers (30x30x350mm). Practice by redrawing a simple table from a photo, then measure a real table and compare. In many African cities, blueprints are used for custom orders; being able to follow them precisely means fewer costly mistakes. If you canât read a drawing, ask for a dimensioned sketch. Use a pencil and ruler to mark key measurements on your own copy. Remember: a good furniture maker checks the drawing twice before cutting once.

lessons.title: Measuring, Marking, and Layout Techniques
lessons.body: Accurate measuring and marking are the difference between a wobbly chair and a solid one. In Africa, where materials can be expensive, wasting wood is not an option. Start with a steel tape measure (5m is standard) and a carpenterâs pencil (flat shape resists rolling). For precision, use a marking knife or a sharp awl to score linesâpencil lines can be 1mm thick, causing errors. Always measure twice, cut once. Use the âburn an inchâ trick: instead of measuring from the zero end (which can be damaged), start at the 100mm mark and subtract 100mm from your reading. For layout, a try square (300mm) checks 90-degree angles. A sliding bevel helps copy angles from a prototype. When marking, use a âwitness lineââa light line first, then darken only after checking. For repeat parts, make a story stick: a straight piece of wood with all measurements marked, so you donât measure each piece individually. In many workshops, a simple bench hook and a marking gauge (for mortise and tenon) are essential. Mark the face side and face edge with a squiggleâthese are your reference surfaces. All measurements should be taken from these faces. For example, when making a table, mark the leg positions from the face edge. Use a sharp pencil and keep it sharpened. In humid African climates, wood moves; measure and mark just before cutting, not hours earlier. Practice by marking out a simple box: 300mm x 200mm x 150mm. Check diagonalsâthey must be equal. If not, your box is out of square. Good marking saves time and material.

lessons.title: Hand Tools: Identification, Use, and Maintenance
lessons.body: Hand tools are the backbone of any African furniture workshop. Start with the essential set: a crosscut saw (for cutting across grain), a rip saw (for cutting along grain), a backsaw (for tenons and joints), a chisel set (6mm, 12mm, 19mm, 25mm), a mallet (wooden or rubber), a hand plane (No. 4 or No. 5), a screwdriver set, a hammer (16oz claw), and a rasp. Learn to sharpen: a dull chisel tears wood. Use a whetstone (1000/6000 grit) with a honing guide. For a 25mm chisel, sharpen at 25 degrees. Test on end grainâit should slice, not crush. Saws need filing: a crosscut saw has teeth angled at 15 degrees, rip saw at 5 degrees. In many rural areas, you can find old saws at markets; restore them with a saw set and file. Maintenance: after use, wipe metal parts with an oily rag (use palm oil or machine oil) to prevent rustâhumidity is the enemy. Store tools in a wooden box with a lid. Chisels should be kept in a roll or with edge guards. A hand plane needs the blade sharpened and the sole waxed (candle wax works) for smooth planing. For a beginner, practice planing a piece of mahogany or iroko: set the blade for a thin shaving (0.2mm). Check flatness with a straightedge. In Africa, many artisans use locally made tools; a well-maintained machete can shape wood, but for joinery, chisels and saws are better. Always cut away from your body. Clamp work securely. A sharp tool is safer than a dull one because it requires less force.

lessons.title: Power Tools: Circular Saws, Drills, Routers, and Sanders
lessons.body: Power tools speed up production but demand respect. In African workshops, a circular saw (185mm blade, 1400W) is common for cutting sheet goods and timber. Always use a sharp blade with the correct number of teeth: 24T for ripping, 40-60T for crosscutting. Set the blade depth to 3mm more than the wood thickness. Use a straight edge or track as a guide. Never cut freehand. For safety, wear goggles and ear protection. A drill (corded or cordless 18V) with bits: twist bits for wood, spade bits for large holes, and Forstner bits for flat-bottom holes. Use a pilot hole for screws to prevent splitting. A router (1200W) with a 6mm or 12mm collet shapes edges, cuts grooves, and makes joints. Common bits: straight, roundover, chamfer, and rabbeting. Set the speed according to bit sizeâlarge bits run slower. Feed the router from left to right (against rotation). A random orbital sander (125mm) with 80, 120, and 220 grit papers smooths surfaces. Start with 80 to remove marks, then 120, then 220. Donât skip grits. In dusty environments, connect a vacuum or wear a dust mask. Power tools need maintenance: blow out dust from motors, check brushes, and keep blades sharp. In many African countries, voltage fluctuates; use a surge protector. For a beginner, practice on scrap wood: cut a straight line, drill a perpendicular hole, rout a roundover, and sand a board. Always unplug before changing blades or bits. Keep cords away from the cutting path.

lessons.title: Wood Joints: Butt, Miter, Dado, Rabbet, and Mortise-and-Tenon
lessons.body: Joints hold furniture together. The butt joint is simplest: two pieces joined at 90 degrees, glued and screwed. Itâs weak alone, so add dowels or a corner brace. A miter joint is a 45-degree cut on each piece, forming a 90-degree corner. Use a miter box or power saw. Glue and nailâbut miters can open; reinforce with splines. A dado is a groove cut across the grain to house a shelf or panel. Cut with a router or dado stack on a table saw. Width should match the shelf thickness (e.g., 18mm). A rabbet is a step cut on the edge, often for cabinet backs. Cut with a router or rabbeting plane. Depth is usually half the wood thickness. The mortise-and-tenon is the strongest: a tenon on one piece fits into a mortise (hole) on another. For a 50mm wide leg, cut a tenon 20mm thick, 40mm long, and 50mm wide. The mortise is chopped with a chisel or drilled and squared. Glue and wedge for extra strength. In Africa, where hardwoods like iroko and mahogany are common, these joints last generations. Practice each joint on scrap wood. For a butt joint, pre-drill to avoid splitting. For a miter, check square with a try square. For a dado, test fitâit should be snug, not loose. For a mortise-and-tenon, mark with a gauge and cut precisely. Always apply wood glue (PVA) and clamp for at least 30 minutes. Remember: a good joint is stronger than the wood itself.

lessons.title: Basic Assembly and Clamping Methods
lessons.body: Assembly is where your furniture takes shape. Start by dry-fitting all parts without glue. Check for square: measure diagonalsâthey must be equal. If not, adjust. Use a mallet to tap joints together, but protect wood with a scrap block. For glue-up, use PVA wood glue (waterproof for outdoor furniture). Apply a thin, even beadâtoo much glue makes a mess. Clamping is critical. Use bar clamps (600mm or 900mm) for large panels, C-clamps for small work, and spring clamps for edges. For a chair, you might need 4-6 clamps. Place clamps alternately top and bottom to distribute pressure. Donât over-tightenâit can starve the joint of glue. For a tabletop, use pipe clamps and check flatness with a straightedge. If you donât have enough clamps, use a rope tourniquet: wrap rope around the piece and twist a stick to tighten. In African workshops, this method is common. For assembly, work on a flat surface. Use a deadman (a vertical support) to hold parts. After clamping, wipe excess glue with a damp cloth. Let it cure for 24 hours before stressing. For drawers, check that they slide smoothly. For doors, ensure they open without rubbing. If a joint is loose, disassemble, clean glue, and add a shim. Practice by assembling a simple box: four sides, glue and clamp, check square. Then move to a stool with stretchers. Remember: patience during assembly saves repair time later.

quiz.q: What do dashed lines represent in a technical drawing?
quiz.explanation: Dashed lines indicate edges that are hidden from the current view.

quiz.q: If a drawing has a scale of 1:10, what does 50mm on paper represent in real life?
quiz.explanation: 1:10 means 1 unit on paper equals 10 units in reality, so 50mm becomes 500mm.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a cutting list?
options: A) To show the final assembled piece
B) To list each part, its dimensions, and quantity
C) To indicate the tools needed
quiz.explanation: A cutting list details all components required for the project.

quiz.q: Why is it recommended to measure twice and cut once?
options: B) To ensure accuracy and avoid material waste
D) To check the tape measure
quiz.explanation: Double-checking measurements prevents costly mistakes and saves wood.

quiz.q: What is the 'burn an inch' trick used for?
options: A) To mark wood with a hot iron
B) To avoid using the damaged end of a tape measure
quiz.explanation: Starting at the 100mm mark and subtracting 100mm avoids inaccuracies from a worn hook.

quiz.q: What does a marking gauge help you do?
options: A) Cut wood at an angle
B) Scribe a line parallel to an edge
C) Measure the length of a board
quiz.explanation: A marking gauge has a pin or knife that scores a line at a set distance from the edge.

quiz.q: Which hand tool is best for cutting along the grain?
quiz.explanation: Rip saws have teeth designed for cutting parallel to the wood grain.

quiz.q: What angle should a chisel be sharpened at for general woodworking?
quiz.explanation: A 25-degree bevel is standard for most chisels used in furniture making.

quiz.q: Why should you oil metal hand tools after use?
options: B) To prevent rust in humid conditions
quiz.explanation: Oil creates a barrier against moisture, which causes rust.

quiz.q: What is the correct blade depth setting for a circular saw?
options: B) 3mm more than the wood thickness
C) 10mm more than the wood thickness
quiz.explanation: Setting the blade 3mm deeper than the wood ensures a clean cut without excessive exposure.

quiz.q: Which drill bit is best for making a flat-bottomed hole?
quiz.explanation: Forstner bits have a sharp rim that cuts a flat-bottomed hole.

quiz.q: When using a router, which direction should you feed the wood?
quiz.explanation: Feeding against the bit rotation prevents the router from grabbing the wood.

quiz.q: What grit sandpaper should you start with to remove marks?
quiz.explanation: 80 grit is coarse enough to remove scratches and plane marks quickly.

quiz.q: Why should you unplug a power tool before changing a blade?
quiz.explanation: Unplugging eliminates the risk of the tool turning on unexpectedly.

quiz.q: Which joint is the strongest for furniture?
quiz.explanation: The mortise-and-tenon provides a large glue surface and mechanical interlock.

quiz.q: What is a dado joint used for?
options: A) Joining two pieces at an angle
B) Housing a shelf or panel
quiz.explanation: A dado is a groove cut across the grain to accept a shelf or panel.

quiz.q: How deep should a rabbet typically be cut?
options: A) One-quarter of the wood thickness
quiz.explanation: A rabbet depth of half the thickness provides a strong shoulder without weakening the piece.

quiz.q: What is a common reinforcement for a miter joint?
quiz.explanation: Splines, dowels, or biscuits can all add strength to a miter joint.

quiz.q: When cutting a mortise, what tool is commonly used?
quiz.explanation: A chisel is used to chop and square the mortise after drilling.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of dry-fitting before gluing?
options: A) To check for square and fit
quiz.explanation: Dry-fitting ensures all parts fit together correctly before glue is applied.

quiz.q: How can you check if a box is square during assembly?
quiz.explanation: Equal diagonals indicate a square assembly.

quiz.q: What type of glue is recommended for outdoor furniture?
quiz.explanation: Waterproof PVA (Type II or III) resists moisture and is suitable for outdoor use.

quiz.q: Why should you not over-tighten clamps?
options: A) It can damage the wood
B) It can starve the joint of glue
C) It can bend the clamps
quiz.explanation: Excessive pressure squeezes out too much glue, weakening the joint.

quiz.q: What is a rope tourniquet used for in assembly?
options: B) To apply clamping pressure when clamps are scarce
quiz.explanation: A rope tourniquet tightens around a piece to act as a clamp.

quiz.q: How long should you let a glued joint cure before stressing?
quiz.explanation: PVA glue reaches full strength after about 24 hours.

quiz.q: What is a deadman in assembly?
options: B) A vertical support to hold parts
quiz.explanation: A deadman is a simple vertical board that supports workpieces during assembly.

quiz.q: Why is it important to wipe excess glue immediately?
options: B) To prevent it from hardening and affecting finish
quiz.explanation: Dried glue is difficult to remove and can interfere with sanding and finishing.

quiz.q: What should you do if a joint is loose during dry fit?
options: B) Use a shim or recut
quiz.explanation: A loose joint needs a shim or recut to ensure a strong glue bond.

quiz.q: Which of these is a safety rule for power tools?
options: B) Keep cords away from cutting path
quiz.explanation: Keeping cords clear prevents tripping and accidental cutting.

quiz.q: What is the first step when reading a blueprint?
options: B) Identify the views and scale
quiz.explanation: Understanding the views and scale is essential before any measurements or cuts.
